title: Double-Scanned Tickets
story: You run the door at a small concert. The scanner logs each ticket code it reads, in the order people walk in. Each ticket is good for one entry, so a code that shows up twice means someone copied a ticket. After the doors close, you want to know whether that happened tonight.
task: Write hasRepeat(codes). Return true if any code appears in the log two or more times, and false if every code is different.
An empty log has no repeats, so return false.

examples.explanation: Code 7788 was scanned at positions 1 and 3. One repeat is enough, so the answer is true.
Four scans, four different codes. Nobody got in twice.
The repeat need not be next to the original: here it came in three people later.

hints: Look at the first example. When the scanner reads the second 7788, what does it need to remember to raise the alarm?
You only need one fact about each earlier code: has it been seen? You do not need to know where it appeared or how many times.
Which structure answers "is this value already in my collection?" in one step?
Walk the log once with an empty set. If a code is already in the set, return true. Otherwise add it. At the end, return false.
bruteForce: Comparing every scan with every later scan takes about n²/2 comparisons, around 5 billion for 100,000 scans. Sorting and comparing neighbours is O(n log n), but still does more work than needed and reorders the log.

js: * @param {number[]} codes  ticket codes in scan order
* @return {boolean} true if any code appears twice

answer at the very start and end

walkthrough: Keep a set of the codes already let in, so checking each new scan is one lookup instead of a search.
• 7788: already in the set. Return true; 5003 is never looked at.
Stopping early pays off: if the copy comes in near the start, you are done almost at once.
solution.timeWhy: One pass, and each set lookup or insert is O(1) on average.
solution.spaceWhy: With no repeats, the set ends up holding every code.
solution.takeaway: To answer "have I seen this before?" while walking a list, keep a hash set of what you have passed. It turns a nested search into one lookup per element.
